lead: An Arduino has no network and a Raspberry Pi cannot promise a pulse to the microsecond. Other boards fill the gaps. The ESP8266 puts a Wi-Fi radio and a small processor on one 3.3 V chip. The BeagleBone Black runs Linux and adds fast real-time co-processors. The pcDuino runs Linux on a board that accepts Arduino shields. This chapter compares all three on five checks: logic voltage, operating system, wireless, pin count and power.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for what an Arduino board is and Chapter 4.3 for Linux boards and 3.3 V GPIO.

blocks.text: The ESP8266 is one chip from Espressif: a 32-bit processor, some memory and a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi radio. A bare module costs a few hundred rupees. The chip runs at 3.3 V and every pin is 3.3 V.

A bare module such as the ESP-01 is awkward: eight pins, no USB socket, and it needs a steady 3.3 V supply while the radio pulls a few hundred milliamps in a transmit burst. Some pins must sit at the right level at boot or the chip starts in the wrong mode.

The NodeMCU board wraps the chip with a USB-to-serial converter, a 3.3 V regulator, two buttons and breadboard headers. You program it from the Arduino IDE after installing the ESP8266 board package; setup() and loop() behave as on an Arduino (see Chapter 4.2).

The radio is why you choose it. The board joins a Wi-Fi network, receives an IP address and can publish a reading straight to a server. Between readings it enters deep sleep: processor and radio off, only a timer running, drawing about 20 µA. That is the chip figure. A stock NodeMCU still draws about a milliamp in sleep because its regulator and USB-to-serial chip keep working.

sections.h3: BeagleBone Black: Linux with fast I/O

blocks.text: The BeagleBone Black is a single-board computer in the same class as the Raspberry Pi (see Chapter 4.3). It boots Linux from 4 GB of on-board flash and has an Ethernet socket, a USB host port and a microSD slot.

Its difference is the header. Two rows of 46 pins give about 65 general-purpose input/output lines, plus analogue inputs, PWM outputs and I2C, SPI and UART buses. All are 3.3 V, and each pin sources only a few milliamps, so a relay or motor needs a driver.

The unusual part is the two PRUs, Programmable Real-time Units. Each is a small 32-bit core at 200 MHz with its own memory, outside the reach of the Linux scheduler. A PRU can hold a pin at an exact rate while Linux is busy with files and network traffic. That is what real-time I/O means here: the timing does not depend on the operating system.
Power comes from a 5 V barrel jack or USB, and the board draws a few hundred milliamps. That rules it out as a battery node and suits it to fixed installations driving many pins with exact timing.

pcDuino is a family of boards built round one idea: run Linux and still accept the shields people already own. The headers are laid out and labelled like an Arduino Uno, so a shield plugs straight in with no wiring.

Inside is an ARM system-on-chip from Allwinner with around 1 GB of RAM, running a full Linux distribution. Control code is written in C or Python on Linux, not as an Arduino sketch. The header pins are wired to that system-on-chip.

Two cautions. The header shape promises mechanical fit, not electrical fit: the pins are 3.3 V and weak, so a 5 V shield can damage the board. And the pin numbers in the vendor library are the vendor's own, so Arduino pin 13 is not automatically the same physical pin.

The gain is one board instead of two: camera, network, storage and physical pins on one Linux machine, with no USB link between a Pi and an Arduino. Some syllabi also list the Cubieboard in this group, another Allwinner-based Linux board, but its GPIO comes out on pin headers rather than an Uno-layout shield socket.
Five checks settle most choices. Work down the list and stop at the first board that passes all five.

items: Logic voltage: match the sensors. A 5 V sensor on a 3.3 V board needs a divider or a level shifter (see Chapter 4.5).
Operating system: no OS means one loop and no files; Linux means Python, files and a network stack, but timing jitter.
Wireless: is Wi-Fi built in, or must you buy a module?
Pins: count GPIO, analogue inputs and buses now, before the design grows.
Power: a battery node wants microamps in sleep; a mains-fed board can draw hundreds of milliamps.

figure.caption: One 60 s cycle of the NodeMCU: 2 s awake at 80 mA, then 58 s asleep at 0.020 mA. The full-width bar is the average drawn over the whole cycle, 2.686 mA — about one-thirtieth of the awake current.

spec.aria: Timeline of one 60 second NodeMCU cycle: 2 seconds awake at 80 mA, 58 seconds asleep at 0.020 mA, and a steady average of 2.686 mA across the whole cycle.

examples.question: An ESP8266 NodeMCU wakes every 60 s. It stays awake for 2 s drawing 80 mA, then sleeps for the rest of the cycle. Use the chip deep-sleep figure of 20 µA. Find the average current drawn from the battery over one cycle.
steps: Sleep current in milliamps: 20 µA = 20 ÷ 1000 mA = 0.020 mA.
Charge used while awake: Q₁ = 80 mA × 2 s = 160 mA·s.
Charge used while asleep: Q₂ = 0.020 mA × 58 s = 1.16 mA·s.
Total charge in one cycle: Q = 160 + 1.16 = 161.16 mA·s.
Cycle time: T = 2 s + 58 s = 60 s.
Average current: I = Q ÷ T = 161.16 mA·s ÷ 60 s = 2.686 mA, so I ≈ 2.69 mA.
examples.answer: The average current is 2.686 mA, about 2.69 mA, which is roughly one-thirtieth of the 80 mA awake current.
examples.check:
awake_mA = 80
awake_s = 2
sleep_uA = 20
cycle_s = 60
sleep_mA = sleep_uA / 1000
sleep_s = cycle_s - awake_s
q_awake = awake_mA * awake_s
q_sleep = sleep_mA * sleep_s
i_avg = (q_awake + q_sleep) / cycle_s
print(round(i_avg, 3))

examples.question: A 5 V sensor output must reach an ESP8266 pin. A divider uses 12 kΩ from the sensor to the pin and 18 kΩ from the pin to ground. What voltage reaches the pin, and is it safe?
steps: Divider rule: Vout = Vin × R_bottom ÷ (R_top + R_bottom).
Sum of resistors: 12 kΩ + 18 kΩ = 30 kΩ.
3.0 V is below the 3.3 V supply. The ESP8266 datasheet high threshold is about 0.75 × 3.3 V = 2.48 V (the 0.7 × VDD = 2.31 V rule is a common CMOS approximation), so 3.0 V is still a safe logic 1.
examples.answer: The pin sees 3.0 V, which is a safe logic high for a 3.3 V input.
examples.check:
vin = 5
r_top = 12
r_bottom = 18
vout = vin * r_bottom / (r_top + r_bottom)
print(round(vout, 2))
print(round(0.75 * 3.3, 3))

traps: ESP8266 and ESP32 pins are 3.3 V and are not 5 V tolerant. The USB socket takes 5 V, the pins do not; a 5 V sensor output needs a divider or level shifter.
A bare ESP-01 is not a NodeMCU board. It has no USB, no regulator and no buttons, and feeding it 5 V destroys it.
An Arduino-shaped header does not mean Arduino voltages. On pcDuino and similar boards the pins come from a 3.3 V system-on-chip, so a 5 V shield can damage the board.
A Linux board does not blink a pin on time. A Python loop on Linux jitters by milliseconds; exact pulses need the BeagleBone PRUs or a small microcontroller.
Header pins source only a few milliamps. A relay coil or motor needs a transistor or driver board, whatever the board costs.

quiz.q: What supply voltage does the ESP8266 need, and what does it draw in deep sleep?
quiz.a: 3.3 V for the chip and all its pins. In deep sleep only a timer runs, drawing about 20 µA.

quiz.q: What does a BeagleBone PRU do that the main Linux processor cannot?
quiz.a: A PRU runs its own fixed loop with its own memory, outside the Linux scheduler, so it toggles pins with exact timing while Linux handles files and network. The main processor's timing depends on scheduling and jitters.

quiz.q: An ESP8266 draws 70 mA for 1 s and 20 µA for 59 s in a 60 s cycle. Find the average current.
A 5 V sensor drives an ESP8266 pin through a divider of 12 kΩ and 18 kΩ (18 kΩ to ground). Find the voltage at the pin and say whether it is a safe logic high.
quiz.a: Vout = 5 V × 18 ÷ (12 + 18) = 3.0 V. The ESP8266 datasheet high threshold is about 0.75 × 3.3 V = 2.48 V (the 0.7 × VDD = 2.31 V rule is a common CMOS approximation), so 3.0 V reads as logic 1 and does not exceed 3.3 V.

quiz.q: A product must run a year on two AA cells, send a Wi-Fi reading every minute and switch one 5 V relay. Which board from this chapter fits, and what extra parts are needed?
quiz.a: The ESP8266 NodeMCU: it has Wi-Fi and deep sleep, and the worked example gives about 2.69 mA average. Check the target: two AA cells store about 2500 mA·h, so average current must stay below 2500 ÷ 8760 h ≈ 0.29 mA. At 2.69 mA the cells last about 2500 ÷ 2.69 ≈ 930 h ≈ 39 days, not a year, so lengthen the sleep interval or use a larger cell. BeagleBone and pcDuino draw hundreds of milliamps and cannot run on AA cells. The relay coil cannot be driven from a 3.3 V pin, so a transistor driver and a 5 V rail are needed, with the pin feeding the transistor base through a resistor.

beyond: Not for the exam. The ESP8266 has largely moved to the ESP32, which adds Bluetooth, a second core and more pins at the same 3.3 V. BeagleBone models now include versions with on-board DSPs and neural accelerators. Small boards such as the RP2040 Pico copy the programmable-I/O idea of the PRUs. Real-time work has also moved into small RTOS kernels such as Zephyr, which runs on many of these boards.
